topic: The Elastic Collision Pi-Calculator: From Physics to Mathematics
target_audience: University students (Physics/Math majors or CS enthusiasts)

sections.title: Introduction: The Paradox of Particles
lecture_lines: Two blocks collide on a frictionless surface.
Mass A is one, Mass B is larger.
How many collisions until they stop moving?
Like a rabbit hitting a massive elephant.
animations: Fade in Title: 'Introduction: The Paradox of Particles' in #FFFFFF.
Create two squares representing block A (mass 1) and block B (mass M). Label them #4DA6FF.
Animate block A moving with velocity v toward stationary block B.
Show impact: A bounces back, B moves forward slowly. Display 'Collision 1'.
Display question 'How many total collisions?' in #FFCC00.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
lecture_lines: Energy and momentum must be conserved.
Elastic collisions preserve total kinetic energy.
Physics maps to a rotation matrix.
animations: Fade in Title: 'Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws' in #FFFFFF.
Write conservation equations: K = 1/2mv^2 and p = mv in #FFCC00.
Animate two particles shifting velocities along a line graph.

sections.title: Connecting Collisions to Pi
lecture_lines: Collisions trace a path in phase space.
The path reflects inside an angular wedge.
High mass ratio creates a circular arc.
Path length approximates the circle's circumference.
This geometric arc reveals digits of Pi.
animations: Fade in Title: 'Connecting Collisions to Pi' in #FFFFFF.
Draw a wedge of angle alpha showing reflected path.
Animate the path becoming a smooth arc for large mass ratio.
Show arc length L proportional to pi.
Highlight points on the arc corresponding to digit values.

lecture_lines: The dance of blocks computes Pi.
